description: Hi, The CSC it is ours
summary:
Field Shift is an accessible, constraint-first crop rotation decision support tool built for irrigated farms across the contiguous United States, centered on the challenge case of Diamond Valley, Nevada—where historical groundwater pumping (~76,000 acre-feet/year) has more than doubled the basin’s perennial yield (30,000 acre-feet/year).

Farmers or local advisers mark any field on a satellite map (or pick from 59 pre-detected Diamond Valley pivots) to pull 36 months of Earth observations from NASA HLS (30 m), SMAP (9 km), NASA POWER (~50 km), SRTM (30 m), OpenET (30 m), USDA CDL, and soil data. A deterministic engine filters out rotations that violate water limits, machinery, planting windows, or buyer availability before five CPU-ready models—trained on 1,138 fields across six western valleys and audited on an unseen valley—compare the current rotation against lower-water and soil-cover alternatives.

Every figure declares its source, date, and native pixel scale; no language model ever invents a number. With WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility, sunlight mode, voice support, and adviser review links, Field Shift turns complex satellite data into transparent, field-ready decisions.
details:
What Field Shift Does and How It Works

Field Shift is a crop rotation decision-support tool for irrigated farms in the contiguous United States, built around the challenge case of Diamond Valley, Nevada (where historical pumping near 76,000 acre-feet/year exceeds the official perennial yield of 30,000 acre-feet/year, NDWR Hydrographic Area 153).

A farmer or local agronomist moves through six clear steps:

  1. Mark the field: Select one of 59 satellite-detected center-pivot fields in Diamond Valley (instant) or click/draw any parcel in the 48 contiguous U.S. states to run an on-demand 36-month Google Earth Engine and NASA POWER analysis (POST /api/v1/analyze).
  2. See the field from space: Inspect a 36-month calendar strip painted with the field’s real monthly Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS, 30 m) color, vegetation/tillage indices (NDVI, NDMI, BSI, NDTI), and crop probabilities read by our temporal-attention GRU neural network alongside Google Dynamic World.
  3. Constraints first: Declare annual water limits, available machinery, planting windows, and crops without a local buyer. A deterministic physical engine (FAO-56 monthly water balance across a 32-crop bank) filters out unviable options first—checking that a candidate meets the water cap even in its highest-use year. If no rotation passes, the tool reports has_viable_options: false and explains which constraint rejected each candidate rather than forcing a recommendation.
  4. Compare three rotations over 36 months: Side-by-side comparison of the current rotation, a lower-water alternative, and a longer soil-cover alternative, showing mean annual irrigation water, months with a living crop, and frost/heat risk days.
  5. Inspect sourced evidence: Each rotation includes an evidence card detailing why it is suggested, supporting observations, benefits, missing information, and local risks that require human verification.
  6. Share and review: Export a print-ready field sheet or generate a private token link where a local adviser can approve, adjust limits, or discard the evaluation—with zero user accounts or personal data collected.

Machine Learning Audited on an Unseen Valley

Rules decide what is feasible; five CPU-ready models estimate what each option means. We sampled 1,138 real irrigated fields across six valleys in Nevada, Utah, and Idaho (2016–2024, 122,904 monthly rows) via Google Earth Engine and held out all of Diamond Valley during training to prevent spatial leakage from neighboring pixels. Every model is reported against its baseline—including the ones that lose:

  • Model 1 · Crop Water Use (XGBoost, no satellite inputs): Predicts monthly evapotranspiration from crop, weather, and soil (20.11 mm/month MAE vs. 25.25 mm FAO-56 baseline on 7,524 unseen field-months, a 20% error reduction), calibrated to each parcel’s observed OpenET level.
  • Model 5 · Crop Sequences (2nd-order Markov chain on USDA CDL 2015–2024): Proposes realistic 3-year crop sequences practiced in comparable valleys (-0.785 log-likelihood vs. -0.938 repeat-last-year baseline across 752 field-years; 78.1% vs. 79.5% top-1 accuracy, both reported).
  • Model 3 · Crop-History Reader (32-unit GRU + Temporal Attention, ONNX): Reads 12 months of HLS indices (0.78 macro F1 on 4-class validation valleys; 0.2716 vs. 0.2439 baseline on 627 Diamond Valley field-years) and highlights which months weighed most in the reading.
  • Model 4 · Regional Soil Moisture Interval (FAO-56 + Leave-One-Valley-Out Conformal Quantile Regression at 90%): Achieves 96.3% empirical coverage vs. 62.0% baseline across 108 SMAP zone-months.
  • Model 2 · Prior-Crop Vigor Effect (XGBoost): Scored -4.6% against its baseline (0.1199 vs. 0.1146 NDVI MAE on 546 field-years). Instead of hiding negative results, Field Shift explicitly states "no local evidence" on screen.

Benefits, Intended Impact, and Creativity

  • Zero Hallucinated Figures: No LLM ever generates water, yield, or savings numbers. Every number carries its provenance card (source, date, native_scale, and type: observed, modeled, or assumed).
  • Strict Scale Honesty: Regional datasets like NASA SMAP (9 km) and NASA POWER (~50 km) are presented strictly as basin context and never disguised as 30 m parcel measurements.
  • Field-First Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA): Built with 18–26 px Atkinson Hyperlegible typography, 44×44 px touch targets for gloved hands, non-color crop patterns, instant U.S./metric unit conversion, a pure black-on-white Sunlight Mode, voice read-aloud/dictation, and a two-layer interactive Guide that tours the UI offline.
  • Dual-Audience Experience: Alongside the clean farmer workbench (/tool), judges can explore an interactive 3D WebGL view of the Model 3 neural network (/), a 3D orbital/terrain showcase with MediaPipe hand-gesture controls (/showcase), an engineer audit console (/engineer), and a QR phone remote (/remote).

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Earth Observation & Data Pipeline: Google Earth Engine (earthengine-api), NASA HLS (30 m), NASA SMAP L4 (9 km), NASA POWER (~50 km), NASA SRTM (30 m), OpenET (30 m), USDA CDL (30 m), USDA NASS QuickStats, SSURGO / ISRIC SoilGrids (250 m).
  • Backend & ML: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, XGBoost, PyTorch (exported to ONNX and served on CPU via onnxruntime), scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, Pytest. Deployed on Railway.
  • Frontend & Testing: Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS (2D/3D DEM terrain), Three.js / @react-three/fiber, @mediapipe/tasks-vision, Web Speech API, Supabase (Postgres + Realtime Broadcast), Playwright + @axe-core/playwright. Deployed on Vercel.
  • Hardware Constraint: Developed on laptops with 8 GB RAM and 6 GB VRAM by offloading heavy spatial reductions to Earth Engine and shipping compact CPU artifacts.
